sweep_summary: Turkish (nucl1301) is in the catalog as fixed-unreviewed (final stress) on Göksel & Kerslake 2005 with an scanned-damaged deciding quote. Of 28 title-matched items, 7 concern Turkish word stress directly, 5 are phrasal/intonational prosody, 6 are other languages or varieties (Anatolian IE, Kabardian, Turkish-German, Early Modern German, English interlanguage) or accent-perception studies, and the rest are unread theory pieces. Read in full this search of works with stress in the title: Özçelik 2014 (held by the project), Özçelik 2016, Bodur et al. 2021, Nagai & Özçelik 2012, Dolatian 2022 (ConCALL-4 proceedings), plus Inkelas & Orgun 2003 (author copy, not a works with stress in the title). Every read source agrees: default primary stress on the final syllable, weight-insensitive, overridden lexically by prespecified roots (Sezer place-name pattern), pre-stressing/stressed suffixes and compounds; Özçelik reinterprets the final prominence as footless intonational prominence, which does not change the placement coding. Recommend replacing the scanned-corrupted Göksel & Kerslake quote with Inkelas & Orgun 2003 p. 140 (or Özçelik 2014 pp. 230-231) as the deciding statement; coding stays fixed: final syllable. Still unobtained (paywalled or print): Kahnemuyipour & Kornfilt 2011, Inkelas 1999/1996, Kabak & Vogel 2011, Kamali & İkizoğlu 2015, Levi 2005 (abstract only), Sezer 1983, Kaisse 1985, Lightner 1978, Nauta 1972; Kan 2009 and Inkelas et al. 2001 not located; Hagberg 2006 open at SIL but could not be reached by automated download.

new_statements.quote: The essential facts of stress in Turkish are these. Every word has exactly one main stress. The default stress position for words is final, e.g. arabá 'car', araba-lár 'car-PL', araba-lar-dán 'car-PL-ABL'; bırák 'leave!', bırak-acák 'leave-FUT', bırak-acak-lár 'leave-FUT-3PL'. Final stress is overridden in words containing lexically stressed roots, lexically stressed or pre-stressing suffixes, certain types of compounds or the type of subconstituent referred to by I&O as a 'Sezer' stem because of its distinctive stress pattern, first described by Sezer (1981). Most compound types have main stress on the first member

new_statements.quote: It is commonly assumed that most Turkish words are stressed on their final syllable, leading to what is generally termed as "regular stress" (e. g. Lees 1961, Lewis 1967, Underhill 1976, Sezer 1983, van der Hulst and van de Weijer 1991, Inkelas 1999, Hayes 1995, Inkelas and Orgun 1995, 1998, Kabak and Vogel 2001). The prosodic word (PWd) is the domain of "stress" in Turkish, and is composed of a root plus all suffixes [...]. Example (1) below illustrates that stress moves to the right each time an additional suffix is added to the PWd, suggesting that it is consistently word-final. Neither the rhyme profile of the syllables involved nor the morphological length of the PWd changes this. [...] (9) Final Prominence: The final syllable of a PWd bears a boundary tone, H%.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Inkelas & Orgun 2003 statement (default final, exceptions lexical/morphological). Adds the claim that regular final prominence is a footless intonational boundary tone rather than metrical stress, that exceptional stress is trochaic, and the secondary-stress and never-final-root-exception details. Supports the catalog's fixed: final syllable coding.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Regular stress falls on the last syllable of the prosodic word (root plus all suffixes) and moves rightward with every suffix; syllable weight and word length are irrelevant. Özçelik's analysis: this regular final prominence is not metrical stress but an intonational boundary tone (H%) on the PWd-final syllable in a footless word; exceptional (non-final) stress comes from lexically footed material (pre-stressing or stressed suffixes, exceptional roots such as place names) parsed into trochaic feet.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Fn. 1 (p. 14): 'Most previous research does not deal with the issue of secondary stress in Turkish'; with more than one foot 'the head of the leftmost foot bears primary stress', the other foot heads carry secondary stress; Özçelik notes secondary stress 'cannot be captured' under Kabak & Vogel 2001 or Newell 2005.
new_statements.exceptions: Pre-stressing suffixes (mostly monosyllabic; a few bisyllabic, §2.1.2.1.1, p. 7), stressed suffixes, and exceptionally stressed roots, mostly place names and loans (§2.1.2.2, p. 9); the Sezer stress rule (antepenult if heavy antepenult and light penult, else penult) is reported as fitting many but not most place names; exceptional root stress is never on the final syllable (p. 17). Regular final stress and exceptional stress have different acoustic correlates.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe standard (Istanbul) Turkish; no dialect is specified. Hagberg's data are taken from Underhill 1976, Sezer 1983 and Kaisse 1985; Özçelik's from the same literature plus his own judgements. Hagberg's SIL 2006 e-book is a republication of the 1993 University of Arizona dissertation; the copy read is the UMI microfilm scan of the dissertation (archive.org), so page numbers are the dissertation's.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's existing statement: default final stress on the suffixed word, with lexical/morphological exception classes (Sezer place-name pattern, one pre-stressing suffix -en, first-member compound stress). Hagberg's inventory of exceptions is narrower than Inkelas & Orgun 2003 (he treats only -en, not the general class of pre-stressing suffixes), but nothing contradicts. Adds the Sezer weight-sensitive rule for the place-name/loan class in full and a note on possible final secondary stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per word, normally on the final syllable (ultima) of the whole word including suffixes; formalised as a word-level stress autosegment linked right-to-left, with no feet in regularly stressed words. Three exceptional classes: (i) place names and loanwords, stressed by the Sezer rule (heavy penult -> penult; light penult + light antepenult -> penult; light penult + heavy antepenult -> antepenult; codas and long vowels count as heavy), analysed as final-syllable extrametricality plus one right-to-left bimoraic foot; (ii) adverbials in -en, with the same footing but opposite linking direction; (iii) compounds (and Sezer's 'emphatic adjectives'), stressed on the last syllable of the first member.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Fn. 20 (p. 163): 'Kaisse 1985 claims that suffixed place names and loan words exhibit secondary stress on the final syllable, as in ankara-dan "from Ankara". Underhill 1976 states that stem stress is unaffected by suffixes in place names and loan words, but he makes no mention of secondary stress.' Hagberg leaves the point open.
new_statements.exceptions: (40) 'Exceptional Stress in Loan Words and Place Names (Sezer 1983): (a) Words with a heavy penult are stressed on the penult. (b) Words with a light penult and a light antepenult are stressed on the penult. (c) Words with a light penult and a heavy antepenult are stressed on the antepenult.' (p. 161, examples lokánta, Vaşington, İstánbul; Kénedi, tornavída; Ánkara type). Adverbials in -en (p. 166-169, after Sezer 1983). Compounds: 'compounds in Turkish are accented on the last syllable of the first member' (Underhill 1976: 117, quoted p. 171). Stress window limited to the last three syllables (p. 178).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: both works read (Özçelik 2017, Hagberg 1993/2006) and the existing Inkelas & Orgun 2003 statement put regular stress on the final syllable of the fully suffixed word, weight-insensitive, with lexical/morphological exceptions (place names and loans following the Sezer weight pattern, pre-stressing suffixes such as -en, compounds stressed on the first member). The sources differ only in analysis: Hagberg treats regular final stress as a word-level stress autosegment linked right-to-left (no feet in regular words), while Özçelik 2017 treats it as an intonational H% boundary tone rather than metrical stress, with feet only in exceptional forms; both are footless for regular words. Hagberg's exception inventory (place names, -en, compounds) is narrower than Inkelas & Orgun's general class of pre-stressing suffixes, which is a difference of coverage, not of placement. On secondary stress, Hagberg reports Kaisse 1985's claim of final secondary stress on suffixed place names (ankará-dan) without endorsing it, while Özçelik 2017 locates secondary stress on the heads of non-leftmost feet in multiply-footed exceptional words; neither bears on the primary placement. Two works (Balcı 2006, Polgárdi 1999) could not be opened.

sources.quote: Regular 'stress' in Turkish falls on the last syllable of prosodic words (PWds), and it is footless. As indicated in (1), each time a suffix is added to a word, stress, or rather prominence, falls on the last syllable of the word: (1) a. eşék 'donkey' b. eşek-lér 'donkeys' c. eşek-ler-ín 'your donkeys' d. eşek-ler-in-dé 'on your donkeys'. Turkish also has some exceptional suffixes that are either pre-stressing or, if bisyllabic, stressed on their first syllable.
